extracted.intended_audience: startup founders, tech PR/communications leads, and early-stage company teams
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for startups and tech companies on crafting memorable messaging, planning launches, building a brand lens, and running PR that earns press and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIBS Test — Relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is your audience, and is your company solving a problem that they care about? What matters to them about that problem? Why does your solution deserve attention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make relevance a priority in your positioning. Fight for greater relevance (example: Salesforce's 'End of Software' reframed the product to appeal to a much larger audience by addressing a broad industry problem rather than feature lists).

rubrics_metrics.name: RIBS Test — Inevitable
rubrics_metrics.description: You want people to feel that whatever you’re developing is inevitable — that the trend or movement you’re part of will eventually come to pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convince reporters and audiences that your idea makes intrinsic sense and could realistically happen; inevitability gives momentum and reduces resistance when persuading press or partners (example: Zuckerberg's belief that technology would connect the world made Facebook feel inevitable).

rubrics_metrics.name: RIBS Test — Believable
rubrics_metrics.description: Convince people that your company is the one that can make the inevitable future happen — that you can carry the ball over the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Believability depends on founders'/team credibility and sustained demonstration over time. It's not enough to be relevant and inevitable; people must trust you can and should win (example: Marc Benioff's background made 'end of software' believable, but it still took years).

rubrics_metrics.name: RIBS Test — Simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep things simple so you can break through attention noise; get messaging to its essence — the one line you want people to remember.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit messaging down to a concise, memorable line (example: 'End of software' — three words). If your messaging isn't unbelievably simple, you're missing the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Launch is an opening move, not the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Launching is like the opening move in a chess game; it doesn't mean that much by itself and is not the be-all-end-all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't 'drop the mic' after launch. Treat launch as the start of a journey and plan follow-up moves to maintain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have both short-term and long-term goals around launch
rubrics_metrics.description: You need both a long-term vision that inspires and short-term milestones that make things happen now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic near-term objectives that are building blocks toward the long-term headline you want; avoid focusing only on improbable 'big' outcomes that don't match current resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your second move before you launch
rubrics_metrics.description: You should only launch if you already know what your second move is going to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan immediate follow-up actions and milestones so launch isn't a one-off; continuous activity 'puts points on the board' and makes the long-term message more believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep beating the drum about your overarching message
rubrics_metrics.description: In everything you do or say and every piece of news you release, you have to keep reinforcing your vision for the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie short-term announcements back to the overarching message so each milestone increases believability of the long-term vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Lens — Tagline (Circle #1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place your tagline at the center of the brand lens exercise as the simplest statement of purpose; if you don't have one, write your company name in the center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is meant to be a simple exercise — don't get sucked into over-optimizing the tagline. Useful but not worth wasting time if it's blocking progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Lens — Attributes (Circle #2)
rubrics_metrics.description: List adjectives and attributes that describe your company; assign them to yourself early so others don't assign them to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid empty words like 'smart' or 'innovative' unless you can argue for them. Attributes should be meaningful and defensible (example: 'moving fast' must be arguable and tied to why it matters for your company).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Lens — Differentiators (Circle #3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the things that set you apart from other companies in the space — your core differentiators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take inventory of differentiators to focus on what matters (example: Salesforce being an online service was a central differentiator; they kept '.com' because it signaled instant online access).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Lens — Action (Circle #4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Run proposed communications/actions through your brand lens to see if they highlight your meaningful words and differentiators; if not, don't do them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the lens to separate internal from external priorities; focus external marketing on where you want to go, what inspires customers, or what matters for success (it may not be what you're selling today).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin — Lust (Don't imitate another brand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't lust after someone else's brand or try to be exactly like them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure out who you are as a founder/brand and be the best at that; comparing yourself is a waste of time and dilutes identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin — Gluttony (Don't try to be all things to all people)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't attempt to serve every audience or stake out every angle; it's impractical and harms focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be selective about who you serve and which stories you pursue externally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin — Greed (Don't let money/attention make you stupid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a lot of money or attention can lead to bad choices and distract from what you actually need to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on what you need to do to succeed rather than pursuing opportunities just because resources allow it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin — Sloth (Don't be lazy in execution or messaging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid lazy moves like 'launching at a conference' as a substitute for real strategy, and don't use buzzwords that become white noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate: don't launch as a lazy tactic; avoid buzzwords such as 'scalability', 'optimization', 'disruption' that add no meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin — Wrath (Don't pick public fights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get into fights with reporters or other brands; it's rarely productive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid engaging in public battles over small details — 'don't wrestle with a pig in the mud.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin — Envy (Don't envy competitors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't keep your eyes fixed on competitors; envy distracts from building your own company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus inward on building your identity and product rather than copying or resenting others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sin — Pride (Don't overreact to press praise or criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: You are never as good or as bad as the press makes you — don't buy into extreme coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat both positive and negative press as potentially distracting; keep perspective and focus on the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit — Be Proactive
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't just answer reporters' questions; tell them what's important about your company and shape the narrative proactively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brand image is malleable; use interviews to introduce key points in every answer because reporters may not know what to ask or emphasize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit — Begin with the end in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the headline you’re aiming for before you start speaking or pitching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure out what the reporter's story will be about and decide what role you want in it ahead of time (example: if the story is about NSA/privacy, plan your place in that story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit — First things first (Set realistic expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Have realistic short-term goals that are achievable with current resources and serve as building blocks toward bigger aspirations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on what you can get now rather than improbable outcomes (example: prioritize achievable media targets before aiming for large national shows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit — Think win-win
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that reporters have needs (clicks, headlines, ad revenue) and position your story so it helps them achieve those goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you lack obvious news elements (ticker symbol, big brand), find angles that make your story interesting to reporters and their audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit — Seek first to understand, then to be understood
rubrics_metrics.description: Be a great listener — absorb what others say before responding, using listening as an opportunity to process and respond thoughtfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listening can yield better, more surprising responses; this habit is credited to effective CEOs like Mark Zuckerberg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit — Synergize (Choose associations wisely)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be conscious of the companies and brands you associate with; strategic associations can help tell your story and gain relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate with super-giants or useful partners when it makes sense to amplify your message, even if they're outside your immediate industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit — Sharpen the saw (Make messaging more resonant over time)
rubrics_metrics.description: You know your messaging is deeply resonant when it gains meaning as time passes and becomes clearer and more impactful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work continuously to refine messaging so it grows more meaningful over years (example: Facebook's 10-year consistency on connecting people became emotionally powerful).
